learn.hook: A steel katori can be a funhouse mirror — look into the inside and outside of the bowl and your face changes!
points: Laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in the same plane. These hold for all reflecting surfaces, including curved ones.
A plane mirror forms an image that is virtual, erect, the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and laterally inverted.
A spherical mirror is part of a hollow sphere. Concave mirrors curve inward (reflecting surface caves in) and converge light; convex mirrors bulge outward and diverge light.

Key terms: pole (P) is the centre of the mirror's surface; centre of curvature (C) is the centre of the sphere; radius of curvature (R) is PC; the principal axis passes through P and C; the principal focus (F) is where rays parallel to the axis meet (concave) or seem to come from (convex).
For mirrors of small aperture, the radius of curvature is twice the focal length: R = 2f, so F lies midway between P and C.

example.q: Think it through: a concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 30 cm. Where is its principal focus?
steps: F lies on the principal axis midway between P and C.
example.answer: The focus is 15 cm from the pole, midway between P and C.

learn.reallife: Torches and vehicle headlights use concave mirrors with the bulb at the focus so that a strong parallel beam is thrown forward.

games.title: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: Centre of the mirror's reflecting surface
Centre of the sphere the mirror is part of
Distance from pole to centre of curvature

Distance from pole to principal focus

games.title: Reflection truth test
items: The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection.
This first law of reflection holds for every reflecting surface.
A plane mirror forms a real image.
A plane mirror's image is virtual; it cannot be caught on a screen.
A concave mirror is a converging mirror.
Rays parallel to its principal axis meet at its focus.
For a spherical mirror of small aperture, R = 2f.
The focus lies midway between the pole and the centre of curvature.
The focus of a convex mirror lies in front of the mirror.
It lies behind a convex mirror; reflected rays only appear to come from it.
The image in a plane mirror is laterally inverted.
Left and right appear swapped, as in 'AMBULANCE' written in reverse on ambulances.

quiz.q: A ray strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 35°. What is the angle of reflection?
quiz.explain: By the first law of reflection, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
quiz.mistake: Measures the angle from the mirror instead of from the normal

quiz.q: The radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is 24 cm. What is its focal length?
quiz.mistake: Doubles R instead of halving it

quiz.q: Which mirror is called a diverging mirror?
quiz.explain: A convex mirror spreads out parallel rays, which appear to come from its focus behind the mirror.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'concave' sounds like spreading

quiz.q: The focus of a concave mirror lies —
options: Midway between the pole and the centre of curvature
quiz.explain: Since R = 2f, F is halfway between P and C, in front of the mirror.
quiz.mistake: Puts F at C

quiz.q: Why is 'AMBULANCE' written in reverse on the front of ambulances?
options: Because the letters are too big
Because convex mirrors make images upside down
So that drivers ahead read it correctly in their rear-view mirrors, which laterally invert it
quiz.explain: Mirrors laterally invert images, so reversed writing appears correct in the mirror.
quiz.mistake: Thinks mirrors invert top and bottom

quiz.q: The line passing through the pole and the centre of curvature of a mirror is called the —
quiz.explain: That line is the principal axis; it is normal to the mirror at the pole.
quiz.mistake: Confuses principal axis with aperture

quiz.q: Which statement about a plane mirror image is correct?
options: It is virtual, erect and of the same size as the object
It is always smaller than the object
It forms in front of the mirror
quiz.explain: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect, same-sized image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
quiz.mistake: Confuses plane mirror images with concave mirror images

quiz.q: The focal length of a spherical mirror is 20 cm. What is its radius of curvature?
quiz.mistake: Halves f instead of doubling it

teach.ask: Gappu stares into a spoon: 'Why do I look upside down on one side and tiny on the other? What's a concave mirror?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The inside of the spoon is concave and converges light; the back is convex and diverges it!
teach.nudge: Good! Which surface of the spoon brings light rays together?

topics.title: Images by spherical mirrors and the mirror formula

learn.hook: Move closer to a concave shaving mirror and suddenly your face becomes giant — the position of the object decides everything!
points: Concave mirror images: object at infinity → image at F (point-sized, real, inverted); beyond C → between F and C (diminished); at C → at C (same size); between C and F → beyond C (enlarged); at F → at infinity; between P and F → behind the mirror, virtual, erect and enlarged.
A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image behind the mirror, between P and F.

New Cartesian sign convention: the pole is the origin; the object is placed to the left; distances measured in the direction of incident light (to the right) are positive, against it negative; heights above the axis are positive. So u is negative for real objects and f is negative for a concave mirror, positive for a convex mirror.
Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Magnification: m = h′/h = −v/u. Negative m means real and inverted; positive m means virtual and erect.
Uses: concave mirrors in torches, headlights, shaving mirrors, dentists' mirrors and solar furnaces; convex mirrors as rear-view mirrors because they give an erect image and a wider field of view.

example.q: A 2 cm tall object is placed 25 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the position and nature of the image.
steps: Sign convention: u = −25 cm, f = −15 cm.
v = −37.5 cm: the image is 37.5 cm in front of the mirror.
Negative m: real and inverted; |m| > 1: enlarged.
example.answer: v = −37.5 cm; the image is real, inverted and enlarged (3 cm tall).

learn.reallife: The curved mirrors at sharp turns on hill roads in Uttarakhand and Himachal are convex: they show a wide view of oncoming traffic.

games.title: Concave mirror: where does the image move?
games.prompt: Object positions from far to near the mirror
items: Object at infinity — image at F
Object beyond C — image between F and C
Object at C — image at C
Object between C and F — image beyond C
Object at F — image at infinity
Object between P and F — image behind the mirror

games.title: Concave or convex mirror?
items: Rear-view mirror of a scooter
Shaving mirror
Dentist's mirror
Headlight reflector
Mirror at a blind turn on a hill road
Solar furnace
Always gives a diminished, erect image

quiz.q: An object is placed at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror. The image is —
options: At C, real, inverted and the same size
quiz.explain: For an object at C, the reflected rays meet at C, giving a real, inverted image of the same size.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the cases for C and F

quiz.q: Which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles, and why?
options: Convex, because it gives an erect, diminished image and a wider field of view
Concave, because it gives a real image
quiz.explain: A convex mirror always gives an erect image and lets the driver see a large area behind.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a magnified image is better for driving

quiz.q: An object is placed 10 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. What is the image distance v (with sign)?
quiz.explain: Positive v means the image is behind the mirror, as expected for a convex mirror.
quiz.mistake: Uses a negative focal length for a convex mirror

quiz.q: A concave mirror forms an image at v = −30 cm of an object at u = −10 cm. What is the magnification?
quiz.explain: m = −v/u = −(−30)/(−10) = −3. Negative m means the image is real and inverted, and it is 3 times the size of the object.
quiz.mistake: Loses track of the minus signs in m = −v/u

quiz.q: Where should an object be placed in front of a concave mirror to get a virtual, erect and enlarged image?
quiz.explain: Only when the object is between the pole and the focus does a concave mirror give a virtual, erect, enlarged image — as in a shaving mirror.
quiz.mistake: Thinks concave mirrors always give real images

quiz.q: In the New Cartesian sign convention, the focal length of a concave mirror is taken as —
options: Positive or negative depending on the object
quiz.explain: The focus of a concave mirror lies in front of it, against the direction of incident light, so f is negative.
quiz.mistake: Thinks focal lengths are always positive

quiz.q: Solving the mirror formula, the magnification of an image comes out as −0.5. The image is —
quiz.explain: Negative m means real and inverted; |m| = 0.5 < 1 means diminished.
quiz.mistake: Reads the sign of m the wrong way round

quiz.q: Why is a concave mirror used by dentists?
options: When held close, it gives an enlarged, erect image of the teeth
It produces a real image on a screen
quiz.explain: With the tooth between P and F, a concave mirror forms an enlarged, virtual, erect image.
quiz.mistake: Thinks dentists use convex mirrors

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do shaving mirrors make faces big but scooter mirrors make cars small?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A concave mirror held close gives an enlarged image; a convex mirror gives a small image but a wider view!
teach.nudge: Good! Which mirror lets the driver see more of the road behind?

topics.title: Refraction of light and refractive index

learn.hook: A coin at the bottom of a bucket of water seems to float up — light is playing tricks as it changes speed!
points: Refraction is the change in direction of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent medium to another, because its speed changes. Light going along the normal does not bend.
Going from a rarer to a denser medium (air → glass), light slows down and bends towards the normal; from denser to rarer, it speeds up and bends away from the normal.
Laws of refraction: (1) the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in one plane; (2) Snell's law — sin i / sin r is constant for a given pair of media and a given colour of light.

Refractive index: n = speed of light in vacuum (c) ÷ speed of light in the medium (v). Relative refractive index n₂₁ = v₁/v₂. Light travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum. Some values: water 1.33, kerosene 1.44, crown glass 1.52, diamond 2.42.

Optical density is not mass density: kerosene floats on water yet is optically denser. In a rectangular glass slab, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways (lateral displacement).

example.q: Think it through: the refractive index of a glass is 1.5. What is the speed of light in it?

learn.reallife: A pencil dipped in a glass of water looks bent at the surface, and a swimming pool looks shallower than it really is — both are due to refraction.

quiz.q: Why does light bend when it passes obliquely from air into water?
quiz.explain: Light travels more slowly in water than in air; this change in speed causes bending.
quiz.mistake: Thinks colour change causes refraction

quiz.q: The refractive index of a glass is 1.5. What is the speed of light in it, in units of 10⁸ m/s?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by n instead of dividing

quiz.q: Which medium in this list is optically densest?
quiz.explain: The higher the refractive index, the optically denser the medium and the slower light travels in it.
quiz.mistake: Confuses optical density with mass density

items: Water
Kerosene
Crown glass
Diamond

quiz.q: A ray of light passes from glass into air. It bends —
quiz.explain: Going from denser to rarer, light speeds up and bends away from the normal.
quiz.mistake: Uses the rule for rarer to denser

quiz.q: What does Snell's law state?
options: sin i / sin r is a constant for a given pair of media
sin r / sin i = speed of light
quiz.explain: For a given colour of light and pair of media, the ratio sin i/sin r is constant — the refractive index.
quiz.mistake: Confuses refraction with the law of reflection

quiz.q: Kerosene floats on water, yet it has a higher refractive index. What does this tell us?
options: Optical density is the same as mass density
Optical density is different from mass density
quiz.explain: Optical density relates to the speed of light in a medium, not to mass per unit volume.
quiz.mistake: Assumes heavier liquids must be optically denser

quiz.q: Light travels in medium 1 at 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s and in medium 2 at 1.5 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1?
quiz.mistake: Divides the speeds the wrong way round

quiz.q: When light passes through a rectangular glass slab, the emergent ray is —
options: Parallel to the incident ray but laterally displaced
Along the same line as the incident ray always
quiz.explain: The bending at the two parallel faces is equal and opposite, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ray exits along the same line

teach.ask: Gappu dips his beak in water: 'Why does my beak look bent? Is the water breaking it?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Light changes speed between water and air, so it bends — refraction makes my beak look bent!
teach.nudge: Good! But why does light bend? What changes when it enters water?

topics.title: Lenses, the lens formula and power

learn.hook: A magnifying glass can make an ant look like a dinosaur — and the same idea helps millions of people see clearly!
points: A convex lens is thicker at the middle and converges light; a concave lens is thinner at the middle and diverges light. Light through the optical centre (O) goes straight on.

Convex lens images: object at infinity → image at F₂ (point-sized); beyond 2F₁ → between F₂ and 2F₂ (diminished); at 2F₁ → at 2F₂ (same size); between F₁ and 2F₁ → beyond 2F₂ (enlarged); at F₁ → at infinity; between F₁ and O → same side as object, virtual, erect, enlarged (magnifying glass).
A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image between its focus and the optical centre, on the same side as the object.
Lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. Magnification: m = h′/h = v/u. Focal length is positive for a convex lens and negative for a concave lens.
Power P = 1/f, with f in metres; unit dioptre (D). A convex lens has positive power, a concave lens negative power. For lenses in contact, P = P₁ + P₂ + …

example.q: An object is placed 15 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the image position and magnification.
steps: v = +30 cm: real image on the other side of the lens.
m = v/u = 30 ÷ (−15) = −2: inverted and twice the size.
example.answer: v = +30 cm, m = −2: real, inverted and enlarged.

learn.reallife: When an optometrist writes −1.5 on your prescription, it means a concave lens of power −1.5 D; a positive number would mean a convex lens.

quiz.q: An object is placed 15 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. What is the image distance v (with sign)?
quiz.explain: v = +30 cm, so a real image forms on the other side of the lens.
quiz.mistake: Adds 1/f and 1/u without using the sign of u

quiz.q: In the same case (u = −15 cm, v = +30 cm), what is the magnification?
quiz.explain: m = v/u = 30 ÷ (−15) = −2: a real, inverted image twice as tall.
quiz.mistake: Uses −v/u, the mirror formula for magnification

quiz.q: What is the power of a convex lens of focal length 25 cm, in dioptres?
quiz.explain: P = 1/f with f in metres: 1 ÷ 0.25 = +4 D.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert centimetres into metres

quiz.q: A concave lens has a focal length of 50 cm. What is its power, in dioptres?
quiz.explain: f = −0.5 m for a concave lens, so P = 1 ÷ (−0.5) = −2 D.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the negative sign for a concave lens

quiz.q: Where must an object be placed in front of a convex lens to get an image of the same size?
quiz.explain: With the object at 2F₁, a real, inverted image of the same size forms at 2F₂.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the 2F and F cases

quiz.q: A concave lens always forms an image that is —
quiz.explain: Whatever the object's position, a concave lens gives a virtual, erect, diminished image.
quiz.mistake: Assumes concave lenses behave like concave mirrors

quiz.q: A lens has a power of −2.5 D. What type of lens is it?
quiz.explain: Negative power means negative focal length, which is a concave (diverging) lens.
quiz.mistake: Thinks power is always positive

quiz.q: Two thin lenses of power +2.0 D and −0.5 D are placed in contact. What is the combined power, in dioptres?
quiz.mistake: Adds the magnitudes and ignores the sign

teach.ask: Gappu looks through Dadaji's magnifying glass: 'How does this make letters bigger? Is it a special lens?'
teach.praise: Chirp! It's a convex lens, and with the letters inside its focal length it makes a virtual, erect, enlarged image!
teach.nudge: Nice! Where must the object be placed for a convex lens to work as a magnifier?
